newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Minister seeks protection for Tanzanian industry.
newsitem.headline: Minister seeks protection for Tanzanian industry.

text.p: Tanzanian Trade and Industry Minister William Shija has called for "selective protection" for key industries against imports.
He spoke as Tanzania and its neighbours, Uganda and Kenya, were proposing to revive a common market that existed until 1977, when the East African Community linking the three countries collapsed.

"I think we should have selective protection of our industries in the future so that they are able to sell at least to the local market," Shija told the Reuters Africa Journal programme in a television interview on Friday.
"Selective protection for industries is done by almost every country I can think of -- that's what we plan to do."

Tanzania's ailing textile industry was one example of the need for protection against low-cost imports. Shija said action would be taken to reduce the volume of textile imports, especially from India and Pakistan.
Many textiles were smuggled in without paying duty, he said.
After a disastrous experiment in socialist planning, begun in 1967, Tanzania embarked on economic reforms supervised by the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in the late 1980s.
Its currency is stable, foreign reserves are up and annual inflation, 25 percent in January 1996, is now 14 percent and falling.

Shija said privatisation and joint ventures were the best way to ensure viability of the state-run textile industry, which had been brought near collapse by poor management and lack of capital. Nationalisation had been a failure, he said.
"We've had experience -- through public ownership we have not done very well and that's why some of our industries have died away," he added.
Although well regarded for its quality, Tanzanian cotton accounts for less than one percent of world production which is dominated by the United States, Australia, China and Russia.
Drought has cut the 1996/97 crop to around 350,000 bales (of 181 kgs) (400 lb) worth about $83 million, against 430,000 bales valued at $109 million the previous year.
Shija was confident the textile industry could be revived within three years. "We think privatisation is the way forward."
